name: Zero
why: This is the smallest input. If your search starts at lo = 1, it can never return 0.

name: One
why: If you start hi at n // 2 to save a step, hi is 0 here, and the answer 1 is outside the window. Starting with hi = n works for every n.

name: Two
why: √2 is about 1.41, so the answer is 1. If you got 2, you returned the first r with r * r >= n, instead of the last r with r * r <= n.

name: Just below a square
why: 4 * 4 = 16 is too big, so the answer is 3. Returning 4 means you found the first T instead of the last T.

name: A perfect square
why: The answer is exactly 4. If you got 3, your test is r * r < n, but it should be r * r <= n.

name: Just above a square
why: √17 is about 4.12, so the answer is 4. If you got 5, the search kept a value whose square is too big.

name: A trillion
why: This is a large perfect square. If this test runs out of time, either the loop steps one value at a time instead of halving, or it gets stuck when two values are left. Lesson 6 explains how to round mid up.

name: Floats get this one wrong
why: `int(n ** 0.5)` and `math.sqrt(n)` turn n into a float, which stores only about 16 significant digits. So n becomes exactly 10**30, and the answer is one too big. Use whole numbers only: compare r * r <= n.

name: A 41-digit number
why: Python integers have no size limit, so a binary search on [0, n] needs only about 133 halvings. If this fails, a float may be used somewhere in your code. Use // for division, not /.

name: Just past 2**53
why: 2**53 + 1 is the first whole number that a float cannot store exactly. So any answer that uses floats is off by one. Only exact whole-number arithmetic gets this right.

name: A huge number that is not a square
why: This number is not a perfect square, and it is far too big for a float to store exactly. The answer is the last r with r * r <= n.
